chapters.line: A journey that never stands still.

chapters.line: The art of keeping what you need.

chapters.name: Skin & defence
chapters.line: A boundary. A community. A defence.

facts.title: You are a community of cells.
facts.text:
Your body is made of tens of trillions of human cells, specialised for different jobs.

A red blood cell carries oxygen. A muscle cell creates force. A nerve cell sends signals. Size and cell counts vary between people; no single number describes every human.

The word "body" describes a living collaboration.

facts.title: Every cell has a border.
facts.text:
A cell membrane is a selective boundary, not a sealed wall.

Its double layer of fats contains proteins that move substances, receive signals and connect cells. Water, ions and nutrients cross in controlled ways, helping the inside stay different from the outside.

Life depends on carefully managed exchange.

facts.title: DNA is information, not a prophecy.
facts.text:
DNA stores instructions used to build and maintain your body.

Its sequence helps cells make proteins and regulate their work. Health also depends on environment, development, chance and behaviour. Having a genetic risk does not always mean a disease will develop.

An instruction is different from an inevitable outcome.

facts.title: Your chromosomes come in pairs.
facts.text:
Most human body cells typically contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.

One set comes from each biological parent. Eggs and sperm usually carry 23 individual chromosomes. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, and chromosome variations occur, so "every cell has 46" is too simple.

The usual pattern has important exceptions.

facts.title: Same DNA. Different jobs.
facts.text:
A skin cell and a nerve cell can use different parts of largely the same genetic instructions.

Gene regulation helps determine which proteins a cell makes. Chemical marks on DNA and its associated proteins can affect gene activity without changing the DNA sequence.

Different pages of the same instruction book are in use.

facts.title: Your cells keep making usable energy.
facts.text:
Mitochondria make much of the ATP that powers many cellular processes.

ATP is an energy-carrying molecule that cells continually use and replenish. Mitochondria also contain a small amount of their own DNA, usually inherited from the mother.

A living cell needs a continuing energy supply.

facts.title: You do not become entirely new every seven years.
facts.text:
Different tissues replace their cells at very different rates.

Some blood and gut-lining cells turn over quickly. Many nerve cells can last a lifetime. Tissue repair also varies, so there is no single date on which your whole body has been replaced.

Renewal happens on many overlapping clocks.

facts.title: Your body is always making adjustments.
facts.text:
Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable ranges.

Feedback systems adjust temperature, blood glucose, water and many other variables. A small change can trigger a response that pushes conditions back toward balance; the target itself may change with circumstances.

Stability is an active process.

facts.title: Nerves use electricity and chemistry.
facts.text:
An electrical impulse can travel along a neuron; chemicals often carry the message to the next cell.

At many synapses, a neuron releases a neurotransmitter into a tiny gap. Receptors on the receiving cell help turn that chemical message into a response.

A thought depends on cells communicating.

facts.title: Insulation helps nerve signals travel.
facts.text:
Myelin wraps around many nerve fibres and helps electrical signals move efficiently.

Gaps between myelin segments allow a signal to be regenerated along the fibre. Damage to this insulation can disrupt communication.

A microscopic covering can change how a whole body functions.

facts.title: Learning can change your brain.
facts.text:
Practice and experience can alter connections and the organisation of brain circuits.

This capacity is called plasticity. Change depends on what is practised, how often, the person's age and other conditions. There is no single fixed timetable for every skill or person.

Plasticity is a capacity, not a countdown.

facts.title: A memory is not stored in one drawer.
facts.text:
Different brain systems contribute to forming and retrieving different kinds of memory.

The hippocampus helps form many new memories. Other networks support skills, emotion and long-term knowledge. Remembering depends on coordinated activity.

Your past is supported by a network.

facts.title: Pain is real, but it is not a damage meter.
facts.text:
Pain emerges from the nervous system's processing of many signals.

Injury can cause pain, but pain can also persist after healing or arise from altered nerve processing. Its intensity does not always match the amount of visible tissue damage.

Pain deserves care even when a scan looks normal.

facts.title: Some reactions take a shorter route.
facts.text:
A withdrawal reflex can begin through spinal circuits before you consciously decide to move.

Sensory neurons carry a signal inward; spinal connections activate motor neurons that move the affected limb. The brain also receives information and can influence reflexes.

Pulling away from heat can start before conscious awareness.

facts.title: Many essential jobs run automatically.
facts.text:
The autonomic nervous system helps regulate heartbeat, digestion, sweating and other functions.

Its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions adjust activity to changing needs. They interact continuously; the body does not live in a permanent "on" or "off" state.

Much of staying alive needs no conscious instruction.

facts.title: Stress is a whole-body event.
facts.text:
The stress response can change breathing, heart rate, muscle tension and hormone release.

It can help you respond to immediate demands. When stress is persistent, repeated activation can affect health. A physical stress sensation is not, by itself, proof that you are in danger.

An alarm is a response; it is not always a prediction.

facts.title: Your eyes start vision; your brain completes it.
facts.text:
Light is focused onto the retina, where specialised cells convert it into electrical signals.

The optic nerve carries those signals to the brain. Seeing depends on this whole pathway, not just on the eye's lens.

You experience a world assembled from signals.

facts.title: Your pupil is an opening.
facts.text:
The coloured iris changes the pupil's size to control how much light enters the eye.

In bright conditions the opening usually becomes smaller; in dim conditions it usually becomes larger. The pupil itself is not a black object inside your eye.

The apparent black circle is a doorway for light.

facts.title: Tears do more than express emotion.
facts.text:
A healthy tear film protects and smooths the surface of your eye.

It includes oily, watery and mucus components that work together. Blinking spreads this film; problems with its amount or composition can cause dry-eye symptoms.

A clear view depends on a very thin wet surface.

facts.title: Hearing begins as movement.
facts.text:
Sound vibrates the eardrum and middle-ear bones, then creates waves in the fluid-filled cochlea.

Sensory hair cells convert that movement into electrical signals. The auditory nerve carries them to the brain.

A voice becomes mechanical motion, then a nerve message.

facts.title: Loud sound can leave permanent damage.
facts.text:
Noise can injure delicate sensory hair cells in the inner ear.

In humans, damaged hearing hair cells do not normally regrow. Risk depends on loudness, exposure time and distance, and a single very intense sound can also cause injury.

Enjoying sound includes protecting the cells that detect it.

facts.title: Balance has more than one information source.
facts.text:
Your brain combines signals from the inner ears, eyes, muscles and joints to help keep you steady.

Inner-ear structures sense head movement and position. Conflicting or disrupted information can contribute to dizziness or unsteadiness.

Standing still is a coordinated sensory achievement.

facts.title: Much of flavour comes through your nose.
facts.text:
Odours reach smell receptors when you sniff and when aromas rise from food during chewing.

Your brain combines smell with taste, texture and temperature. A blocked nose can therefore make a meal seem strangely flat.

Taste and flavour are related, but they are not identical.

facts.title: The old tongue map is misleading.
facts.text:
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami are not restricted to separate tongue zones.

Taste cells for these qualities are distributed across taste-bud-containing regions. Sensitivity can vary, but the tip is not the only place that detects sweetness.

Your tongue is not divided into five exclusive territories.

facts.title: Your heart is two pumps working together.
facts.text:
The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side sends it around the body.

Its four chambers and valves organise this movement. The muscular left ventricle supplies the pressure needed for the larger body circuit.

The lungs and the rest of the body are connected in a loop.

facts.title: A heartbeat starts with an electrical signal.
facts.text:
Specialised heart cells generate and conduct the signals that coordinate a beat.

The sinoatrial node normally sets the rhythm. Nerves and hormones can speed or slow it, while the heart's own electrical network organises the sequence.

Your heart has a built-in timing system.

facts.title: Arteries and veins are named by direction.
facts.text:
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood. Oxygen content alone does not define either kind of vessel.

The exception disappears when you follow the direction.

facts.title: The smallest vessels do the exchanging.
facts.text:
Capillaries form fine networks between the arterial and venous sides of circulation.

Their thin walls allow oxygen, nutrients and wastes to move between blood and surrounding tissues. The large vessels transport; these tiny vessels bring the delivery close.

A delivery network needs local access.

facts.title: Your blood carries oxygen using iron.
facts.text:
Haemoglobin inside red blood cells binds oxygen with the help of iron-containing groups.

Red cells load oxygen in the lungs and deliver it to tissues. Having too little healthy haemoglobin can reduce oxygen delivery and contribute to fatigue.

Iron matters because of the job it helps a protein do.

facts.title: Blood cells are made inside bones.
facts.text:
Blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow produce red cells, many white cells and platelets.

These products have different jobs: oxygen transport, defence and clotting. The soft tissue inside certain bones is therefore essential to your circulating blood.

Your skeleton contains a blood-cell factory.

facts.title: A clot is a coordinated repair.
facts.text:
Platelets gather at an injured blood vessel, while clotting proteins help form a stabilising fibrin mesh.

This process limits bleeding. Clotting in the wrong place can block blood flow, so the body also needs ways to control and remove clots.

A useful repair depends on the right place and timing.

facts.title: Blood type is about recognition.
facts.text:
ABO and Rh blood groups describe important markers on red blood cells.

An incompatible transfusion can trigger a dangerous immune reaction. Matching involves more than casually knowing one letter, and clinical testing remains essential.

Blood compatibility is a medical check, not a guess.

facts.title: Blood pressure contains two different moments.
facts.text:
The upper number describes pressure when the heart contracts; the lower number describes pressure between beats.

These are systolic and diastolic pressure. Readings vary with conditions and technique, so diagnosis usually needs properly taken, repeated measurements.

A reading describes force in the arteries, not how stressed you feel.

facts.title: Breathing starts by changing space.
facts.text:
When your diaphragm contracts, it moves down and helps enlarge the chest cavity.

Pressure inside the lungs falls, drawing air in. At quiet rest, breathing out is mostly driven by relaxation and elastic recoil.

Air follows a pressure difference.

facts.title: Your lungs trade gases across thin walls.
facts.text:
Tiny air sacs called alveoli sit beside networks of capillaries.

Oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves into the air sacs, down their respective concentration-related pressure gradients. The thin interface makes this exchange possible.

The important meeting is between air and blood.

facts.title: Breathing clears a waste gas, too.
facts.text:
Your cells produce carbon dioxide as they use energy from nutrients.

The brain and other sensors monitor carbon dioxide, acidity and oxygen-related signals to help regulate breathing. Breathing is about removing carbon dioxide as well as bringing in oxygen.

The outward breath is part of the same essential exchange.

facts.title: Your nose prepares incoming air.
facts.text:
The nasal passages help warm, moisten and filter air before it travels deeper.

Mucus and tiny hairs help trap particles. This preparation supports the respiratory tract, though it cannot remove every pollutant or germ.

The entrance to your airway also does useful work.

facts.title: Your airways have a moving clean-up layer.
facts.text:
Mucus traps particles, while tiny cilia help move it toward the throat.

This clearance system helps protect the lungs. Tobacco smoke can damage airway defences and contribute to lung disease.

Some of your cleaning equipment is microscopic and constantly moving.

facts.title: Your voice is shaped breath.
facts.text:
Air from the lungs passes through the voice box, where the vocal folds can vibrate.

The throat, mouth, nose and tongue help shape that sound into speech. Strain, illness and irritation can affect this delicate system.

Speaking is a collaboration between airflow and moving tissue.

facts.title: Movement makes your breathing work harder.
facts.text:
Active muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, so breathing and circulation increase.

Regular physical activity helps the heart and lungs work more efficiently. Fitness develops through repeated activity rather than a single deep breath.

The lungs work as part of a larger delivery system.

facts.title: Digestion begins before food reaches your stomach.
facts.text:
Chewing breaks food apart, and saliva moistens it and starts chemical digestion.

Saliva also supports swallowing and helps protect the mouth. It is an active fluid rather than simply water that happens to be there.

The first digestive juice is already in your mouth.

facts.title: Food does not simply fall through you.
facts.text:
Waves of muscle activity move and mix material along the digestive tract.

This process, called peristalsis, helps transport food through the oesophagus and intestines. Gravity can help, but coordinated muscle movement does the organised work.

Your digestive tract is an active tube.

facts.title: Your stomach needs protection from its own acid.
facts.text:
A protective lining normally helps shield stomach tissue from acid and digestive activity.

Helicobacter pylori infection and certain pain medicines can damage defences and contribute to peptic ulcers. An ulcer is not simply the result of "too much worry."

A strong digestive environment needs a protected boundary.

facts.title: Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine.
facts.text:
After food is broken into smaller molecules, the intestinal lining transfers nutrients into circulation.

Its folded surface and specialised cells support absorption. The stomach helps prepare a meal; the small intestine does much of the collecting.

Eating a nutrient and absorbing it are different steps.

facts.title: The pancreas supplies a digestive toolkit.
facts.text:
The pancreas sends enzymes into the small intestine to help break down fats, proteins and carbohydrates.

This is separate from its hormone-producing role. If too few digestive enzymes reach the intestine, the body may struggle to digest and absorb nutrients.

One organ can have two very different kinds of output.

facts.title: Your liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores it.
facts.text:
Bile helps the digestive process handle fats and absorb some vitamins.

The gallbladder releases stored bile into the small intestine. The liver also processes and stores absorbed nutrients, helping manage what becomes available to the rest of the body.

The factory and the storage pouch have different jobs.

facts.title: Some fibre feeds the microbes in your gut.
facts.text:
Humans do not digest dietary fibre in the same way as starch or sugar.

Some fibre is fermented by gut microbes; other forms add bulk or help with stool consistency. Different fibres have different effects, which is one reason food variety matters.

A meal can nourish both you and your resident microbes.

facts.title: Your gut and brain communicate in both directions.
facts.text:
Nerves, hormones and other signals link digestion with the nervous system.

This helps explain why stress can change bowel symptoms and why digestive discomfort can affect how you feel. These symptoms are physical, even when stress is involved.

A brain-gut interaction does not mean "imaginary."

facts.title: Tooth decay is a process, not a sudden hole.
facts.text:
Mouth bacteria can turn sugars into acids that remove minerals from enamel.

Saliva and fluoride help the enamel regain minerals in early stages. Repeated acid attacks can eventually create a cavity that needs treatment.

A cavity has a history before it becomes visible.

facts.title: Your kidneys filter, then make choices.
facts.text:
Each kidney contains many filtering units called nephrons.

Blood is filtered at the glomerulus. Tubules then return needed water and substances to the blood while helping remove wastes. Urine is the result of this processing.

A kidney is more selective than a kitchen sieve.

facts.title: Water and salts are managed together.
facts.text:
The kidneys adjust how much water and how many dissolved substances leave in urine.

This helps keep blood chemistry and fluid volume within useful ranges. The right balance changes with heat, activity, illness and other conditions.

Water balance is also chemistry balance.

facts.title: Kidneys also send important chemical messages.
facts.text:
They help regulate blood pressure, support red-blood-cell production and activate vitamin D.

These jobs connect kidney health with circulation, blood and bones. Their role reaches well beyond making urine.

A filtering organ is also a signalling organ.

facts.title: Your bladder stores urine, not your kidneys.
facts.text:
Urine travels from the kidneys down the ureters into the bladder.

During urination it leaves through the urethra. Muscles, nerves and the brain coordinate storage and emptying; ureters and urethra are different structures.

Two similar-sounding words describe different parts of the route.

facts.title: There is no perfect water quota for everyone.
facts.text:
Fluid needs change with age, activity, temperature, pregnancy, illness and what you eat.

Drinks and water in food both contribute. For many people, pale-yellow urine is a useful rough clue, but medicines and other factors can alter colour. Some medical conditions require individual fluid advice.

Hydration is a changing need, not a universal bottle count.

facts.title: Too much water can also cause harm.
facts.text:
Drinking excessive water faster than it can be removed can dilute blood sodium.

Sodium helps regulate fluid balance and nerve function. Severe low sodium can be dangerous, which is why forcing very large amounts of water is not a reliable health habit.

More is not automatically better.

facts.title: Dehydration has clues you can notice.
facts.text:
Thirst, darker urine, urinating less and dizziness can occur when you lose more fluid than you replace.

Sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea can increase losses. Symptoms and risk vary, and significant dehydration needs medical attention.

Water loss changes how the whole body works.

facts.title: Bone is living tissue.
facts.text:
Specialised cells continually remove old bone and build new bone.

This remodelling helps maintain the skeleton and manage minerals. Bone has a blood supply and responds to hormones, nutrition and mechanical demands.

Your framework is being maintained from within.

facts.title: The adult skeleton usually has 206 bones.
facts.text:
That is the standard anatomical count, not an identical total in every person.

Some bones fuse during growth, and small additional bones can vary between people. The skeleton supports movement and protects important organs.

An anatomical number describes a typical pattern.

facts.title: Many joints use a low-friction meeting surface.
facts.text:
In a typical freely moving joint, cartilage covers the ends of bones and fluid helps them move smoothly.

The surrounding capsule, ligaments and muscles contribute to stability. Different types of joints allow different kinds of movement.

Movement depends on the surfaces between bones, too.

facts.title: Tendons and ligaments do different jobs.
facts.text:
Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments usually connect one bone to another.

These strong connective tissues help transmit force and stabilise joints. Their names are not interchangeable, even though both can be injured.

One transfers a muscle's pull; the other helps secure a joint.

facts.title: Muscles create force by pulling.
facts.text:
Within skeletal muscle, organised protein filaments interact to generate tension.

The muscle transfers force through its attachments and can move or stabilise a joint. A muscle can also work without visibly shortening, such as when you hold a position.

Visible movement is only one kind of muscle work.

facts.title: Many movements need opposing muscle groups.
facts.text:
To bend and straighten a joint, the nervous system coordinates muscles with different pulling directions.

At the elbow, the biceps helps bend the arm and the triceps helps straighten it. Their activity is coordinated rather than simply one being completely on and the other off.

Control comes from teamwork, not strength alone.

facts.title: Bones respond to being used.
facts.text:
Weight-bearing activity and resistance exercise help stimulate bone maintenance.

The benefit depends on the kind of activity, age and health. Nutrition and hormones matter too; exercise is one contributor rather than a guarantee against fractures.

Mechanical demand is information for living bone.

facts.title: Next-day soreness is not trapped lactic acid.
facts.text:
Unfamiliar exercise can lead to delayed muscle soreness that develops hours later.

It involves responses to exercise-related tissue stress, especially after certain lengthening contractions. Lactate does not remain trapped in muscles for days to explain this soreness.

Soreness is not a reliable score for a good workout.

facts.title: Your skin is a working boundary.
facts.text:
It helps limit water loss, blocks many outside threats and detects sensations.

Its layers contain different cells and structures, including nerves, glands and immune cells. The surface you see is part of a much larger protective system.

Skin is an organ doing several jobs at once.

facts.title: Melanin offers protection, but not complete protection.
facts.text:
This pigment contributes to skin colour and helps protect cells from ultraviolet radiation.

Every skin tone can be damaged by UV exposure. Skin colour changes the degree of natural protection; it does not remove the need to protect skin.

A tan is not a shield against all sun damage.

facts.title: Sweat cools you when it evaporates.
facts.text:
Evaporation carries heat away from the skin.

High humidity can make this cooling less effective because sweat evaporates less readily. Heavy sweating does not, by itself, prove that a workout is better or that fat is melting away.

The cooling happens as liquid becomes vapour.

facts.title: You have a second fluid-return network.
facts.text:
Lymphatic vessels collect excess fluid from tissues and help return it to the bloodstream.

Lymph nodes contain immune cells that examine material travelling through this network. Lymph vessels also help transport absorbed fats from the intestine.

The lymphatic system supports both fluid balance and defence.

facts.title: Your immune system has immediate and learned defences.
facts.text:
Innate responses act rapidly; adaptive responses recognise specific targets and can form memory.

These systems work together. A healthy response needs regulation as well as strength, because uncontrolled immune activity can damage your own tissues.

Good defence depends on a suitable response, not endless activation.

facts.title: Vaccines prepare immune memory.
facts.text:
Vaccination exposes the immune system to a safe form, part or set of instructions related to a pathogen.

This can help it respond more effectively during a later encounter. Protection and the need for further doses vary by vaccine and infection.

Preparation can happen before the real exposure.

facts.title: An allergy is a misdirected immune response.
facts.text:
The immune system reacts to a substance that is harmless to most people.

Food allergy differs from food intolerance, which does not necessarily involve the same immune mechanism. Allergic reactions can vary from mild symptoms to life-threatening anaphylaxis.

A powerful defence can sometimes identify the wrong target.

facts.title: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections.
facts.text:
They act against bacteria, not the viruses responsible for colds and flu.

Unnecessary antibiotic use can cause side effects and helps drive antibiotic resistance. A bacterial complication is a separate reason a clinician might prescribe one.

The cause of an illness matters to the treatment.

facts.title: Hormones are messages with specific receivers.
facts.text:
They travel through the bloodstream and act on cells with suitable receptors.

They help regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction and many other processes. The effect depends on the hormone, its concentration and the receiving tissue.

A circulating message does not make every cell respond alike.

facts.title: Insulin helps manage blood glucose.
facts.text:
Made in the pancreas, insulin helps glucose move from the blood into many cells for use or storage.

Diabetes develops when the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use it properly. Different types of diabetes have different causes.

Blood sugar regulation involves both a signal and a response.

facts.title: The thyroid influences the pace of body processes.
facts.text:
Thyroid hormones affect how the body uses energy and influence many organs.

Too little or too much can affect heart rate, temperature tolerance and other functions. Symptoms overlap with many conditions, so a symptom alone cannot diagnose a thyroid disorder.

A small gland can have effects throughout the body.

facts.title: Puberty begins with a signalling conversation.
facts.text:
Signals from the brain and pituitary stimulate the ovaries or testes to make more reproductive hormones.

These changes contribute to sexual maturation, growth and other physical changes. Timing and pace differ between people.

Development follows a process, not a race.

facts.title: A menstrual period is the shedding of a lining.
facts.text:
Hormones help the uterus build a lining in preparation for a possible pregnancy.

If pregnancy does not occur, hormone changes lead to shedding through the vagina. The cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.

The bleeding is one part of a larger cycle.

facts.title: Ovulation does not always happen on day 14.
facts.text:
Ovulation is the release of an egg from an ovary.

Cycle length and ovulation timing vary, including within the same person. A calendar estimate alone cannot reliably identify every fertile day or rule out pregnancy.

A textbook day is not a universal biological appointment.

facts.title: An egg and a sperm each usually bring 23 chromosomes.
facts.text:
Fertilisation combines their genetic material to begin a new developmental process.

Sperm are produced in the testes after puberty. Reproduction depends on multiple steps, including gamete production, transport and, for pregnancy, successful implantation.

One meeting is the beginning of a complex sequence.

facts.title: The placenta is a temporary, essential organ.
facts.text:
During pregnancy, it supports exchange of oxygen, nutrients and wastes between the pregnant person's circulation and the developing baby's circulation.

These circulations normally remain distinct. The placenta also makes hormones and is not a perfect barrier against medicines, infections or harmful exposures.

A temporary organ can sustain an entire new life.

facts.title: Menopause is a transition in reproductive function.
facts.text:
Natural menopause is recognised after 12 consecutive months without a period when there is no other cause.

The years around it can involve changing hormone levels, irregular cycles and symptoms such as hot flushes. Experiences differ, and symptoms can be treated.

A normal life transition still deserves individual care.

facts.title: Sleep is a changing pattern of brain states.
facts.text:
During a typical night, you cycle through non-REM and REM sleep.

Deep non-REM sleep and REM sleep have different features, and their proportions change across the night and across life. Sleep is not simply the brain being switched off.

Your sleeping brain follows an organised night shift.

facts.title: Sleep helps learning become more lasting.
facts.text:
Sleep supports processes involved in stabilising memories and learning.

Both non-REM and REM sleep appear to contribute. Staying awake longer to practise or study can come at the cost of the sleep that supports what you learned.

Learning continues after the book closes.

facts.title: Light helps set your internal clock.
facts.text:
A daily timing system helps organise sleepiness, alertness and hormone rhythms.

Light reaching the eyes is a major cue for this clock. The timing of light matters, so bright light late in the evening can shift sleep timing.

The body reads light as information about time.

facts.title: Sleep needs change with age.
facts.text:
Most adults are advised to get 7 to 9 hours a night; teenagers generally need 8 to 10.

Children usually need more. Individual needs and circumstances vary, and time in bed is not always the same as restorative sleep.

The right sleep target is not identical at every age.

facts.title: Caffeine changes the feeling of sleep pressure.
facts.text:
Adenosine builds up during waking hours and contributes to sleepiness; caffeine interferes with its signalling.

Caffeine can make you feel more alert without removing the need for sleep. Its effects can last for hours and vary between people.

Feeling less sleepy is different from being fully rested.

facts.title: Alcohol can make sleep less restorative.
facts.text:
It may make falling asleep feel easier while disturbing sleep later in the night.

It can also worsen breathing problems during sleep. Sedation and healthy sleep are not interchangeable.

Falling asleep quickly is only one part of a good night.

facts.title: Breathing pauses during sleep deserve attention.
facts.text:
Sleep apnoea involves repeated interruptions of breathing while asleep.

Loud snoring, observed pauses and daytime sleepiness can be clues, though not every snorer has apnoea. Assessment matters because repeated interruptions can affect health and alertness.

A person may sleep for hours and still have disrupted sleep.

facts.title: Waking and muscle control can briefly get out of step.
facts.text:
Sleep paralysis can happen while falling asleep or waking, when you feel awake but cannot move or speak.

It is linked to the muscle inhibition of REM sleep continuing into awareness. Episodes can feel frightening; recurring or distressing symptoms merit medical advice.

A vivid experience can have an explanation in sleep physiology.

facts.title: Regular movement benefits far more than muscles.
facts.text:
Physical activity supports cardiovascular health, mental health and many other aspects of well-being.

For most adults, WHO recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or an equivalent amount of vigorous activity. Some activity is better than none, with adaptations to ability and health.

Benefits begin before you become an athlete.

facts.title: Strength matters throughout adulthood.
facts.text:
Muscle-strengthening activity supports physical function and complements aerobic movement.

WHO recommends it on at least two days a week for adults, involving the major muscle groups. What is suitable depends on a person's abilities and health.

A useful movement plan includes both endurance and strength.

facts.title: No single food can do the work of a varied diet.
facts.text:
A healthy eating pattern supplies different nutrients from a range of foods.

Vegetables, fruits, pulses, whole grains and suitable protein sources can all contribute. The overall pattern matters more than declaring one ingredient a miracle or a villain.

Food variety helps cover different biological needs.

facts.title: You use energy even while resting.
facts.text:
Maintaining cells, circulating blood, breathing and regulating temperature all require energy.

Body size, composition, age, hormones and activity influence energy needs. Daily requirements are therefore not identical between people or constant throughout life.

Resting does not mean metabolically inactive.

facts.title: Fever is a regulated rise in temperature.
facts.text:
During fever, the body's temperature-control system raises its target.

This differs from overheating caused by excessive heat or failed cooling. Infection is a common cause of fever, but the temperature alone cannot identify a specific infection or tell whether antibiotics are needed.

A thermometer gives information, not the whole diagnosis.

facts.title: Feeling fine does not measure blood pressure.
facts.text:
High blood pressure often causes no noticeable symptoms.

Over time, it can damage blood vessels and organs. A properly taken measurement can reveal a problem that your day-to-day sensations do not detect.

Some important body information has to be measured.

facts.title: Ageing is not one identical process in everyone.
facts.text:
Body composition commonly changes with age, including changes in muscle, fat and body water.

The pace and effects differ between people. Activity, nutrition, health conditions and other factors shape function, so chronological age does not describe every ability.

A birthday is not a complete biological assessment.

facts.title: Cancer begins in the body's own cells.
facts.text:
Changes in genes that regulate growth and division can allow cells to grow out of control.

Some cancer-related changes are inherited; many arise during life. Cancers differ greatly, and a cancer being "genetic" does not mean it was necessarily inherited.

Genetic and inherited are not the same word.

facts.title: Sudden neurological changes can be an emergency.
facts.text:
A stroke can cause sudden facial drooping, arm weakness, speech trouble, vision changes or loss of balance.

Urgent treatment can limit damage. Seek emergency help immediately, even if the symptoms fade; do not wait to see whether sleep or rest fixes them.

Sudden change is the signal to act quickly.

facts.title: A heart attack does not always look dramatic.
facts.text:
Symptoms may include chest pressure, breathlessness, sweating, nausea or pain in the arm, back, neck or jaw.

They can begin mildly and vary between people. Suspected heart-attack symptoms need emergency medical help; do not wait for severe pain or drive yourself.

Knowing the quieter signs can change what happens next.
